title: COSY Sightings: The Language of the First Day
dek: Where this month’s words turned up in ordinary places — a bookshop till, a school gate, a bakery counter.

blocks.text: Sightings is the part of the magazine where the language stops being homework. This month we looked for the vocabulary of beginning: enrolment, timetable, term, register, first day.

A bookshop at a station in Lyon, the first week of September: a hand-written card above the till reading c’est la rentrée. Not a slogan — a fact of national life, with its own grammar. La rentrée is a noun for an event everyone attends.

A school gate in Athens at twenty to eight: a grandmother telling a child μην αγχώνεσαι, do not stress yourself. The verb is αγχώνομαι, to be strangled by anxiety. English says “don’t worry”; Greek names the thing around your throat.
A bakery in Naples the same week: si ricomincia, we start again — said by the baker about the school run, not about the bread.

Sightings are also a test of the hundred-word list. If the list is doing its job, a beginner should recognise a good share of what a city says in September: open, new, first, day, time, start. If most of a sign is still opaque, that is information too — not a failure, but a measurement of where you actually are, taken in the street rather than in a test.

items: A1–A2: Find one sign in your target language this week that uses a word from the hundred-word list. Photograph it or copy it.
B1–B2: Which word did you meet in the street before you met it in a lesson? What did you assume it meant?
C1–C2: What does your city’s vocabulary of September reveal that a textbook would leave out?
A1–A2: Copy three words from signs this week. Say each one out loud before you look it up.

blocks.title: This could be a good research question
blocks.content: Do learners who record words seen in public spaces remember them longer than learners who meet the same words in a vocabulary list?
